cards.title: Rabies elimination
cards.author: Muhammad Aftab Gohar
cards.why: It gives rich, quote-worthy public health data for essays on health governance, provincial administration, and human development.
cards.summary: Rabies claims thousands of lives in Pakistan each year despite being entirely preventable. Widespread dog bites and poor diagnostic awareness cause many cases to go untreated until symptoms turn fatal. Overcoming this crisis requires better disease tracking, accessible care, and targeted animal control.
key_facts: Sindh recorded 285,000 dog-bite cases in 2025 and over 200,000 cases by September 2026, causing at least 41 confirmed rabies deaths in 2026.
Punjab logged more than 1.3 million dog-bite cases between 2021 and March 2026.
Estimates place total annual rabies deaths in Pakistan between 2,000 and 5,000 people, with children forming a large share.
A study published in eBioMedicine detected the rabies virus in 64 out of 100 severe dog-bite wounds examined in Karachi.

vocab.meaning: close observation and monitoring of disease spread or activity

text: IT begins with a fever, a headache and a restlessness that will not settle. Then the patient panics at the sight of water. After days of going from hospital to hospital, the family learns that a dog bite weeks or months earlier, long healed and forgotten, carried rabies. The virus has reached the brain, and there is no cure.

This scene plays out in hospitals across Pakistan every week, yet every such death is preventable. Sindh, where reporting has improved, recorded 285,000 dog bites in 2025 and over 200,000 by September 2026, with at least 41 rabies deaths this year. The Indus Hospital also saw rabies cases from Balochistan, and eight more came through teleconsultation from across the country. Punjab reported more than 1.3 million dog-bite cases between 2021 and March 2026. Estimates put Pakistan’s rabies deaths at 2,000 to 5,000 a year, most of them poor and many of them children.

A study published this year in eBioMedicine, a Lancet journal, which I co-authored with Indus Hospital and Erasmus MC colleagues, shows how widely the virus circulates. We found rabies virus in 64 of 100 severe dog-bite wounds in Karachi, and two-thirds of the patients were children. It covered only severe bites, so it does not mean two in three biting dogs are rabid, but the warning is stark. If this is the picture in a city with the province’s best-equipped bite clinics, it is unlikely to be better elsewhere in Sindh or Pakistan.

Elimination needs action on five fronts. The first is surveillance. Behind every reported case is a grieving family. Much of the recent rise reflects improved surveillance, and the true burden is still hidden. Many families believe the patient is possessed and turn to a shrine, not a hospital; others die in hospital undiagnosed. Surveillance must keep improving, with human rabies and dog bites notifiable at every level, so that reliable data reveals the true burden and where to focus resources. Swabbing bite wounds can also track the virus without catching dogs.
Vaccine and immunoglobulin must be free at every public facility.

The second is awareness. Children, especially boys, often tease street dogs and cannot defend themselves when attacked; peaceful coexistence starts with how we treat community dogs. Every household should know to wash a bite wound with soap and running water for 15 minutes, then seek immediate treatment at an anti-rabies centre, since washing reduces the virus but does not remove it. These messages belong in school curricula, mosques and the media.

The third is correct treatment. Rabies is almost 100 per cent preventable with timely post-exposure prophylaxis, and in our study nearly 96pc of patients developed protective antibodies. Yet roughly half of the rabies deaths reported at our centres occur in people whose treatment was incomplete or wrongly given. Immunoglobulin remains scarce, and too many patients drop out before finishing the course. Vaccine and immunoglobulin must be free at every public facility, and every doctor and nurse treating bites must be trained to WHO guidelines. The Sindh government’s ongoing rabies campaign deserves credit and, if sustained, can save many lives.

The fourth is mass dog vaccination, because treating people alone will never end rabies. When at least 70pc of dogs are vaccinated year after year, the virus stops circulating. In September 2026, WHO validated Bhutan as the first country in WHO’s South-East Asia Region to eliminate dog-transmitted human rabies.

The fifth is effective dog population management. Uncollected garbage feeds street dogs, which is why katchi abadis have the most dogs and the most bites. Views differ on the best methods, but any approach must be hu­­mane, gu­­i­ded by evidence and international standards, sustained over time, and backed by proper waste management and responsible ownership. Local governments, veterinary services and communities must agree on what works locally and monitor results.

None of this can succeed in isolation. Health, livestock, local government and education departments each hold a piece and must work together under the One Health approach. The federal health minister’s in-principle approval of a National Rabies Prevention and Control Framework in July 2026 offers real hope. With timely notification, sustained funding and clear, measurable targets, it could become the turning point Pakistan has long awaited, with the media and civil society holding every institution to account.
The global goal is zero deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030. Bhutan has shown it can be done. A rabies-free Pakistan is within reach if we act together, and act now.

The writer is technical lead, Rabies Prevention, Management & Training Services at the Indus Hospital & Health Network, Pakistan, and part of the National & Provincial Technical Working Advisory Group on Rabies.
Published in Dawn, November 17th, 2026

cards.title: Peace prognosis
cards.author: Dr Raashid Wali Janjua
cards.why: It provides critical context and figures on terrorism havens and regional security for Pakistan Affairs and Foreign Policy papers.
cards.summary: The Afghan Taliban continue to harbor and sustain militant groups that threaten regional peace. External financial support and cross-border illicit trades help keep the regime and its allied networks afloat. Despite past diplomatic outreach, Kabul avoids acting firmly against outfits operating on its territory.
key_facts: Since August 2021, donors have confirmed paying $8 billion in humanitarian assistance to Afghanistan through international bodies.
An additional $3.78 billion has been committed and $94 million pledged by international donors for Afghan humanitarian assistance.
Militant outfits mentioned operating under the Afghan regime's umbrella include Al Qaeda, IS-K, ETIM, and the TTP.

vocab.meaning: a policy of seeking to recover lost territory
stubborn refusal to change one's opinion or course of action
favorable or likely to produce success

text: AFGHAN foreign and domestic policies are a curious mix of tribalism, revanchism and ideological confusion that shun human rights and statecraft in favour of support for terrorist groups based on Afghan soil that pose a clear danger to regional peace. Unfortunately, all attempts at positive engagement with the Afghan Taliban by Pakistan as well as regional countries have been scuttled due to Kabul’s lack of willingness to rein in terrorist outfits operating under its benign gaze.

A belief has gained traction amongst the Afghan Taliban that their successful armed struggle against Nato/USA could also be emulated by their ideological comrades like Al Qaeda, IS-K, ETIM, the TTP etc in pursuit of their political objectives. Rooted in medieval notions of tribal honour and revenge, the regime offers a propitious environment for growth of terror networks. The flow of external funds into the Afghan regime’s coffers has encouraged the obduracy of the Taliban, which continues channelling these funds to its ideological allies, sustaining the vicious cycle of terrorism and crime.

Afghanistan is acting as a generous host for terrorist outfits that use its soil to generate economic rents through narco-trafficking, ransom, and smuggling. These groups are confident that their base of operation and sources of income would remain protected under the Taliban. A mere look at the figures showing the funding of this terror haven by the unsuspecting international community indicates why Taliban-ruled Afghanistan remains a threat.

Since August 2021, donors have confirmed paying $8 billion in humanitarian assistance to Afghanistan through various international organisations, with a further $3.78bn committed and $94 million pled­ged. Billions more were reportedly received by the Taliban regime in direct foreign grants. Western capitals remain the biggest financial contributors to Afghanistan.
The Afghan economy is kept afloat by foreign patronage and narco-trafficking.

Afghanistan imports goods worth around $12bn annually against exports of only $1.7bn, leaving an annual trade deficit of $10.3bn. It is intriguing how the Taliban regime is bridging $10.3bn every year. The answer lies in $17.5bn in foreign grants received since 2021, besides billions of dollars earned through narco-trafficking. It is clear evidence of an economy kept afloat by foreign patronage and narco-trafficking.

But the biggest question is: should such a regime that hosts terrorist groups be kept afloat through the largesse of international donors who might soon feel the heat from violent groups based in Afghanistan? If the international community thinks it can wean the Afghan Taliban away from terrorists, it needs to have a look at Pakistan’s 17 sincere attempts through ministers, the national security advisor, special representative, and joint coordination committee interactions, besides internationally mediated parleys in Doha, Istanbul, Riyadh and Urumqi.

The reason for Afghan obstinacy is hubris and ideological narcissism that are pampered through foreign indulgence, despite zero concessions by the Kandahar-based ruling clique on political inclusivity, women’s education and minority rights. Pakistan has tried bilateral channels and has exhausted relevant regional fora like the trilateral group (Pakistan, China and Afghanistan) where in 2023 the Afghan foreign minister agreed to stop the flow of terrorism from Afghan soil.

The Moscow Format , which evolved out of a quadrilateral forum which was abandoned by the US after the Ukraine War, kept pressing the Afghan regime to abide by international counterterrorism obligations till its seventh meeting. However, it failed to elicit a positive response from the Taliban delegation during its eighth iteration at Mos­cow on Oct 5.

The Taliban’s reluctance to even acknowledge the need to stop the ac­­tivities of terrorist groups from Afghan soil betrays a mindset that is sympathetic to these violent groups. This should be a clear message to countries like Russia that are giving space to the Taliban regime in pursuit of narrow security goals.

The fact is that all development and connectivity goals like TAPI, Casa-1000, and Trans-Afghan Railway, as well as mines and mineral exploration in Afghanistan, would remain a pipe dream till the time the Afghan Taliban stop sponsoring terrorism.

The proceeds from illegal mining go to support the Taliban’s military infrastructure. Moreover, since 2021, it has established thousands of madressahs against 269 modern schools, replaced 90,000 teachers with around 100,000 Taliban-aligned clerics, abolished 18 university disciplines, rewritten 200-plus subjects and banned 679 textbooks.
Until the Taliban regime gives up its support for terrorism and provides verifiable guarantees to Pakistan, meaningful normalisation, regional connectivity and lasting stability will not materialise.
The writer is a PhD from NUST.

Published in Dawn, November 17th, 2026

cards.title: Being civil to begin with
cards.author: Jawed Naqvi
cards.why: It highlights options for informal diplomacy and trade between Pakistan and India within multilateral forums like the SCO.
cards.summary: Pakistan decided to send a minister to the SCO Civilisational Dialogue in New Delhi on November 20. Such multilateral interactions could help reduce bilateral friction even under rigid political settings. A workable thaw could mirror quiet, unannounced trade openings rather than sweeping diplomatic announcements.
key_facts: Pakistan is sending a federal minister to attend the SCO Civilisational Dialogue in New Delhi on November 20.
Analyst Trita Parsi proposed the Swiss cheese model to describe low-key, informal relaxations of economic restrictions without formal policy reversals.

cards.title: Films and politics
cards.author: Arifa Noor
cards.why: It offers an analytical angle on public perception and extrajudicial police practices relevant to criminal justice essays.
cards.summary: Popular media often reflects public applause for extrajudicial police encounters after heinous crimes. The film Daayra highlights how public sentiment celebrates instant vigilante justice over formal judicial due process. This dynamic complicates efforts by human rights bodies and internal affairs teams to enforce the rule of law.
key_facts: Daayra is an Indian OTT film focused on the investigation of extrajudicial police encounters following a violent crime.
